$description: A machine you read at three in the morning: the whole instrument is dark glass and lit figures, the values are the loud part, the labels stay quiet, and the panel's own light is the only illumination in the room. The day shift is the same machine under a lavender lamp — the same shapes, the same space, a different light.

color.$description: One hue family for the surfaces and one signal for everything that speaks. The ramp is an indigo ink — never a warm charcoal, because a warm dark stops reading as a screen — and the lit colours are the only saturated things on the panel. Every step below is restated for the daylit face; a step means the same thing in both lights.

neutral.$description: Ten steps of the same indigo ink, restated for the other light. The meaning of each step does not change — 50 is always the page, 900 is always the ink — so a mode is a change of light, not a change of system.

50.$description: The page: the panel itself. The ink the console is built out of, and the floor every other surface is measured against.

100.$description: One step towards the light: a card, a popover, a menu — anything that sits on the page rather than in it.

200.$description: One step away from the light: the trough a field is cut into, the stripe under a table row. A field is cut out of the panel, never laid on top of it.

300.$description: The fill a dead control wears: the panel switched off. Still a surface, no longer asking to be pressed.

400.$description: A soft rule: a divider a shade stronger than the hairline, for the place where a panel is divided in two.

500.$description: The strong edge in the panel's own ink: a frame that has to be seen against the surface it is drawn on.

600.$description: The second voice: captions, helper copy, the small print that still has to be read.

700.$description: A faint ink: a placeholder, a value that has not arrived yet, a column that is empty on purpose.

800.$description: A second ink, one step under the body: a sub-heading, a figure's caption, a label that has to sit under something louder.

900.$description: The ink: body text. Ninety-five percent of a white, never pure white, so a page of values does not flare.

primary.$description: The electric cyan: the one colour that acts. It is the primary button, the link in running text and the focus ring, and it is spent on nothing else — a second loud colour would mean the first one means nothing.

on-primary.$description: The ink on the acting colour: the console's own black, because at night the cyan is a light rather than a pigment. In daylight the same slot takes a near-white, because the deep magenta is a pigment there.

secondary.$description: The quiet fill: a violet panel a step off the page, for a control that is present but not asking for attention.

on-secondary.$description: The ink on the quiet fill: a pale violet in the night, a deep violet under the day lamp.

accent.$description: The signal: hot magenta, the colour the console uses when it has something to say. It is the accent badge, the alert's leading edge and the little marks on a panel — never the button.

on-accent.$description: The ink on the signal: the console's own black. A lit plate is cut, not painted, so its label is the dark that was behind it — and in the day shift the teal is a deep plate instead of a lamp, so it takes paper.

semantic.$description: The console's other four lamps. Each is a brighter neighbour of the signal rather than a colour imported from another theme, and each is answered with an ink of its own so a filled badge is never a label on a colour nobody chose.

success.$description: The green lamp: a thing that worked. Bright at night, like the cyan it sits beside; a deep plate by day, so it can still be read as a word on pale paper.

warning.$description: The amber lamp: a mark that wants to be read before it is acted on. The warmest thing on the panel, and still well under the signal.

error.$description: The fault lamp: a vermilion, warmer and more orange than the signal, so a danger and a mark are never the same word on a panel.

info.$description: The blue lamp: the cyan's own cousin, and the only other colour on the panel that carries a hue of its own.

on-semantic-success.$description: The ink on the green lamp: the console's own black at night, because a lamp that reads as a word on a night panel is a lit lamp and takes the dark ink.

on-semantic-warning.$description: The ink on the amber lamp. Amber is a light colour in both shifts, so it always takes the dark ink — a white label on a lit lamp is a label nobody can read.

on-semantic-error.$description: The ink on the fault lamp: the console's own black at night, because a vermilion that bright is a lit lamp and takes the dark ink like the other three. The day shift's vermilion is a deep plate instead, so it takes paper.

on-semantic-info.$description: The ink on the blue lamp: the console's own black at night, the paper of the day shift by day.

on-danger.$description: The legacy name for the ink on the fault fill. It points at `color.on-semantic-error` — the role the contract requires and the floor is measured on — so the two names can never disagree.

surface.$description: The page. The ink the console is built out of at night; pale lavender paper in the day shift. Same step, same meaning, different light.

surface-raised.$description: A surface that sits above the page: cards, popovers, menus, the secondary button. It is one step towards the light and carries no shadow of its own.

surface-sunken.$description: A surface that sits below the page: the stripe under a table row, the trough a field is carved into.

field.$description: A field's own surface: the trough cut into the panel. A field is an object you can put a cursor in, and it is cut into the page rather than laid on it.

text.$description: Body text: ink on panel, panel on ink.

text-muted.$description: The second voice: captions, helper copy, the small print that still has to be read.

border.$description: The hairline. A rule here is a cool white laid down at a sixth of its strength, so a divider reads as a pencil line on the glass rather than a drawn box.

border-strong.$description: A control's own edge: the acting colour at four tenths, the line a finger has to find. It carries three to one against the page, or the control is not a control.

scrim.$description: What dims the page behind a modal: the console's own black, laid over the panel.

disabled.$description: The fill a dead control wears: the panel switched off. A control that cannot be pressed is still printed — it is simply printed in the quiet ink.

on-disabled.$description: The ink on that fill: the second voice, the one the small print is set in. Dimming the control would dim this with it, and the label is the one thing a dead control still has to say.

focus-ring.$description: The acting colour, and only the acting colour: the ring never wears a colour that means something else, and never the vermilion of a fault.

link.$description: The acting colour, as a word in running text. A link is never the body ink — a link you cannot pick out of the prose is a link nobody clicks — and it is never the vermilion, so a link and a danger are never the same word.

spacing.$description: A tight scale for a dense instrument: the small steps are the inside of a control, the middle steps carry a card, and one roomy step is reserved for the gap between two sections of a page.

1.$description: The inside of a control: the gap between a key's label and its own edge.

2.$description: The small gap: a control's own block padding, and the space between a label and the value under it.

3.$description: The gap inside a panel, one step above the small gap.

4.$description: The body's own step: a card's air inside, and a control's inline padding.

5.$description: Between a caption and the thing it captions.

6.$description: The gap that carries a panel: the space a card gives its own parts.

7.$description: Between two rows of a specimen.

8.$description: The gap between two blocks on a page — where this theme puts its emphasis instead of putting a box around them.

10.$description: A section's own air, top and bottom.

12.$description: The space a page gives a section it means.

16.$description: The gap between two sections of a page.

20.$description: The macro gap: the air between a page and the section it is about to leave.

24.$description: The last step: the air a page opens with, and closes with.

32.$description: The empty space a poster would need. A control room never gets there.

font.$description: Three voices, each with a job: a geometric sans carries the prose, an angular technical display speaks only where a heading may speak, and a mono carries every value that is measured rather than read.

sans.$description: The body voice: a geometric sans with a squared-off skeleton, so a caption at eleven pixels still reads as a word and a paragraph at fourteen still reads as prose.

heading.$description: The display voice: an angular technical face, cut with flat terminals and open apertures. It speaks in headings and nowhere else — a panel's title is a heading, a page of values is not.

body.$description: The prose face: the sans under another name, so a page reads whole.

mono.$value: JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace
mono.$description: The value voice: a developer mono whose figures line up in a column. Numbers, identifiers, timings, log lines — everything a reader measures rather than reads.

serif.$description: The reading face, and the only one in the theme that belongs to the reader rather than to the panel: it is used where a document is quoted instead of reported. The platform's serif, named here so the choice is the theme's and not the browser's.

brand.$description: The logotype face: the values face, stamped on the panel the way a machine's plate is stamped on its case.

size.$description: Eight steps, dense at the bottom and wide at the top, with the jump at the top a scale rather than an increment.

2xs.$description: The printed caption: the smallest step on the console, for the label that sits under a value.

xs.$description: The label on a control, and the caption under a figure.

sm.$description: Secondary text in a dense column, and the size every table reads at.

md.$description: The body. Fourteen pixels, because this is a reading surface before it is a poster.

lg.$description: A lead-in line: the sentence that introduces what follows.

xl.$description: A section head, sized to be found rather than to be impressed.

2xl.$description: The head of a section that has to carry a column on its own.

3xl.$description: A page's own head. Two and a half times the body, and the one step where the jump is a scale rather than a font size.

weight.$description: Four weights, and the middle two do the work: an instrument is read, not admired.

regular.$description: The body: prose at its own weight.

medium.$description: A label that has to hold its own against the value under it.

semibold.$description: The weight of a label: the weight helm's tracked captions wear, and the weight a control carries over the prose around it.

bold.$description: A heading that has to win a page.

letter-spacing.$description: How far the letters sit from each other. The panel's own captions are tracked open so a label sits on the page like a rule; the prose is left alone.

tighter.$description: The display tracking: a heading closes up by a hair so its edges stay sharp.

normal.$description: Body copy, values, and anything unlabelled.

wide.$description: The printed caption: the label above a field, the heading of a column.

wider.$description: A word set as a label on a machine: tracked open enough that the letters read as separate marks, the way helm's terminal captions do.

widest.$description: A single word carrying a whole section. Poster spacing.

radius.$description: Sharp instrument radii: a console is cut, not moulded. The ladder is two, four and seven pixels, and the pill is there for the one control that really is a switch.

none.$description: The faceplate: a card, a table, a frame. A console panel is cut square, and the edge of one is a line rather than a curve.

sm.$description: A hair off square: the plate a message is printed on, the tag a status is stamped in.

md.$description: The working radius: a button, a field, a card — the cut objects a finger meets.

lg.$description: The overlay's corner: the one surface that is clearly a different object from the page under it.

full.$description: The pill: a switch's knob, and the one tag that says something soft.

opacity.$description: How much of a thing is shown, as a fraction. A short ladder, because the same fraction reads differently over glass than over paper.

10.$description: A ghost: present in the DOM, gone from the eye. Reserved for decoration.

25.$description: A wash: an overlay's own veil, laid over the panel without hiding it.

40.$description: The dimmed step: a placeholder image, a track before it is filled, a hint of content.

50.$description: The dim a dead control wears on a value that is running rather than waiting: the only opacity in the theme that spends on a control, and it spends on the whole of it, so the label dims with the fill.

100.$description: Fully shown. The default, named so a rule can say it rather than assume it.

shadow.$description: Neon on ink: every shadow is a coloured halo with a crisp core under it, because the light in this room comes from the screen. Nothing is drawn with a diffuse cloud, and nothing casts one on a card that does not float.

sm.$description: The card's own rest: a hair of shadow and a cyan hairline around the edge. A panel is separated by its outline, not by a cloud under it.

md.$description: The raised panel: the console's own black under the edge, and the signal's halo around it. A magenta glow under a surface is this theme's whole idea of depth.

lg.$description: The overlay: a dialog floating over the console, with the signal's halo around it. It is the only thing in the theme allowed to be this loud.

breakpoint.$description: The widths where the layout steps change, named for what changes there.

sm.$description: Where a single column of readings becomes two.

md.$description: Where a row of panels becomes a grid of panels.

lg.$description: Where a rail of controls becomes a row above the page.

xl.$description: Where four screens can be compared side by side without any of them being squeezed.

z-index.$description: Stacking order, spaced so a layer can be inserted between two without renumbering the world.

motion.$description: The accent moves and the rest does not. Motion points; it does not perform — no overshoot, no bounce, and one loop in the whole theme.

fast.$description: A state change the reader has already decided to expect: a hover, a press, a focus, a spinner.

base.$description: The default: a colour or a rule moving to its next position, and the longest a panel may take to settle.

slow.$description: The longest a transition may take: a panel arriving, a rule settling.

loop.$description: The loop: the pulse, the shimmer, the one thing on the console that moves without being asked. It is the only duration that runs on its own, and it is a step of its own so the slowest transition does not have to carry it — well above the floor below which a loop reads as a strobe.

linear.$description: No curve at all, for motion that is a loop rather than a gesture.

standard.$description: The default curve: it leaves at once and settles slowly, the way a switch on a console throws and then stops.

decelerate.$description: An entrance: the element arrives and stops, without a bounce at the end.

accelerate.$description: An exit: the element leaves, and the curve carries it out of the frame.

button.$description: The voice of the primary control: a lit key set in the panel's own label voice, with the acting colour under it and nothing over it.

weight.$description: The button's own weight. A control carries more weight than the prose around it, and 600 is the last step before it starts shouting.

case.$description: A key says what it does, in the case it is written. A theme that set every button in capitals would have a page of capitals, which is a shout and not a voice — and the buttons are not the only thing on the page.

tracking.$description: The label's own tracking: a machine's caption is tracked open, so a control reads as a stamped plate rather than as a sentence. It is the one place the tracking scale's widest ordinary step is spent.

shadow.$description: Nothing at rest. The key is moulded into the panel, not laid on it, and a shadow would make it a photograph of a key.

shadow-hover.$description: The lit halo the key wears when it is touched: the acting colour, blooming once around the edge. The only shadow a control casts, and it is light rather than matter.

border.$description: Stroke weight, in whole pixels: a console renders a hairline at one pixel or it has stopped being a console.

width.$description: The hairline every control and surface draws with — the thread itself.

width-2.$description: The emphasis edge: a control that must read as selected rather than merely bordered.

width-4.$description: The heavy edge. Rare on purpose — a stroke this thick is a statement, not a divider.

width-8.$description: The frame. A block drawn rather than outlined.

focus.$description: The focus ring, shared by every interactive element: buttons, links, fields, summaries and dialogs. Its colour is the acting colour, so the ring never argues with the ink around it.

width.$description: The ring's stroke. Two pixels in both lights: a one-pixel ring reads as a rendering artifact rather than a decision.

offset.$description: The gap between the ring and the control it is on — far enough that the ring is drawn on the panel and never on the fill it is meant to be reading against.

icon.$description: Glyph sizes, in `em`, so a glyph tracks the control it sits in.

sm.$description: The smallest glyph step: a mark beside a caption.

md.$description: The default glyph step, the size of the label it sits beside.

lg.$description: The largest glyph step: a mark on its own, or the face of a switch.

badge.$description: The small tag, and what shape it is: a square plate, because a status on this console is a stamp on a panel rather than a soft word on a pill.

edge.$description: The stroke the badge draws around itself, so a small shape holds apart from the page it sits on.

pill.$description: Not a pill. A tag on a machine is a rectangular plate with a hairline around it; the round one is for words that are soft, and nothing on this console is soft.

checkbox.$description: How physical a checkbox is: one scalar driving three inset shadows. Zero is flat and drawn, and in this theme it is zero because the light in this room comes from the screen, not from the controls.

switch.$description: The same question as the checkbox, asked of a different control, and answered the same way: the switch is drawn onto the panel too, so a lit switch beside a drawn checkbox cannot happen.

avatar.$description: How big an avatar is, as the edge of the square it fills.

sm.$description: The size for a face in a list or a comment: it reads beside its label without leading the row.

md.$description: The default: a face beside a name, or a profile header at rest.

lg.$description: A face as the subject of a page: a profile header at the top of a long column.

card.$description: The card's own decisions: its corner, its air, its edge, its elevation. A card is a panel on the panel, and it is held off the page by a hairline of light rather than by a cloud.

radius.$description: Four pixels: a card is a faceplate cut out of the sheet, and it is cut with a small chamfer rather than a curve.

padding.$description: The air inside the card, between its parts and around its edge.

border.$description: The ink of the card's own edge: the page's hairline, because a rule is all that separates one thing from the next here.

elevation.$description: The card's rest: the console's own black under the edge, the signal's halo around it, and a cyan hairline on top. The card floats by its outline and its halo, not by a cloud under it.

alert.$description: The alert's own decisions: its corner, its air, and the ink of the hairline it wears. The tone recolours one edge of the same frame, so a fault and a notice are the same object in two colours.

radius.$description: Two pixels: a message is a plate printed on the panel, and it is not the panel itself.

padding.$description: The air above and below the message — more of it than beside it, because the text is read in a line.

padding-inline.$description: The air beside the message, where it is read.

edge.$description: The ink of the hairline on every side. The tone variants recolour the leading edge alone, so this one is the quiet frame around them.

field.$description: The field's own decisions: its corner and the ink of its edge.

radius.$description: The cut corner: a field is an object a finger finds, so it is cut like a key and sunk into the panel like a trough.

border.$description: The line a finger has to find: the acting colour at four tenths, one step stronger than the dividers around it, or the control is not a control.

stat.$description: The stat's own decisions: the number it shows, and how that number is set.

value-size.$description: The size of the number: twice the body, because the number is the point of the stat and the label under it is not.

value-weight.$description: The weight of the number: enough to be read at a glance, not enough to shout. A figure in this theme is a reading, and a reading is set in the mono.

value-family.$description: The face the number is set in: the mono, because a figure is a figure and the mono is the face that carries figures — the digits line up down a column of readings.

table.$description: The table's own decisions: the weight of a column's heading, the ink of the rule under a row, and the fill a striped row wears.

header-weight.$description: The weight of a heading: heavier than the row beneath it, so the column names itself without a rule of its own.

rule.$description: The ink of the rule under a row: the page's hairline.

zebra.$description: The fill a striped row wears: one step below the page, so a reader can hold their place across a wide table without the stripes becoming a pattern to look at.

link.$description: The link's own decisions: the rule under it.

underline.$description: A hair, the width of the rule the rest of the theme draws with. A link is a word on the page, not a sticker on it.
